n: Now God explains the “parable” of the forest fire in plain terms. (Hebrew Bibles number this as 21:6.)

f.w: the word of the LORD came unto me

n: Ezekiel faces Jerusalem, its sanctuaries, and the land of Israel. The “south forest” of chapter 20 is now named outright.

f.g: The temple and its courts.

n: God draws his sword against the land, cutting off both righteous and wicked. Invasion would sweep up everyone, though God still knows his own (9:4).

f.w: will draw forth my sword out of his sheath

f.g: In war, physical suffering falls on all, though eternal judgment remains individual.

n: Because both will be cut off, the sword will sweep the whole land from south to north—the “green and dry trees” of 20:47.

f.w: from the south to the north

n: Everyone will know the Lord drew this sword, and it will not be put back until its work is done.

f.w: it shall not return any more

n: Ezekiel must groan as if his body were breaking, bitterly and in public—another acted sign.

f.w: with the breaking of thy loins
f.g: With a groan that seems to come from his very core.

n: When people ask why he groans, he answers: “Because of the news that is coming.” Every heart will melt, hands go limp, and knees turn to water.

f.g: The news of Jerusalem’s fall (see 33:21).

n: A new message follows: “the Song of the Sword.”

f.w: Again the word of the LORD came unto me
f.g: Verses 8–17 are a fierce poem.

n: “A sword, a sword, sharpened and polished!” The repetition builds dread.

f.g: Polished.

n: It is sharpened for slaughter and polished to flash like lightning. Should anyone celebrate? The sword scorns the royal scepter of Judah as if it were just another stick.

f.g: Is this a time for rejoicing? No.
Probably Judah’s royal scepter; the Hebrew is very difficult.

n: The sword is handed over polished and ready for the slayer—Nebuchadnezzar.

f.g: The executioner—Babylon’s king.

n: Cry and wail, Ezekiel, for the sword is aimed at God’s own people and their leaders. Slapping the thigh was a sign of grief.

f.g: A gesture of mourning and dismay.

n: It is a time of testing. What if even the scepter is rejected? It will be no more—Judah’s kingship will end.

f.w: what if the sword contemn even the rod?
f.g: The Hebrew is obscure; it seems to say the scepter itself will be despised and removed.

n: Ezekiel claps his hands as the sword strikes again and again—a sword for great slaughter that reaches even into private rooms.

f.w: let the sword be doubled the third time
f.g: Let it strike twice, three times—repeatedly.
Inner, private rooms.

n: The sword’s point is at every gate, so hearts fail and many fall. It flashes like lightning, drawn for slaughter.

f.w: it is wrapped up for the slaughter
f.g: Gripped, ready to strike.

n: The sword is addressed: slash to the right, to the left, wherever you are aimed.

f.g: In whatever direction you are pointed.

n: God himself claps his hands, and his anger will be satisfied.

f.w: I will cause my fury to rest

n: A new message with another acted-out sign.

f.w: The word of the LORD came unto me again
f.g: This oracle pictures Babylon’s king choosing his target.

n: Ezekiel draws a road map: two routes branching from one land, with a signpost at the fork pointing toward the cities.

f.g: Mark out two roads.
Literally “cut a hand”—a signpost.

n: One road leads to Rabbah, capital of Ammon (modern Amman, Jordan); the other to fortified Jerusalem. Both had rebelled against Babylon.

f.g: Rabbah, the Ammonite capital, today Amman, Jordan.

n: At the fork, Nebuchadnezzar seeks omens: shaking arrows, consulting household idols, and examining a sacrificed animal’s liver—common Babylonian methods of divination.

f.g: Belomancy—drawing marked arrows from a quiver like casting lots.
Hebrew teraphim, household idols.
Hepatoscopy—reading omens from an animal liver, a common Babylonian practice.

n: The omen in his right hand says “Jerusalem.” He orders commanders forward, battle cries, battering rams, siege ramps, and siege walls. God uses even a pagan king’s fortune-telling to accomplish his purpose.

f.w: to appoint battering rams against the gates

n: Jerusalem’s people will think the omen is false because of their treaty oaths. But the king will remember their rebellion, and they will be captured.

f.w: to them that have sworn oaths
f.g: Those who had sworn loyalty to Babylon and then broken it.

n: Because their sins are now out in the open for all to see, they will be taken captive.

f.w: ye shall be taken with the hand
f.g: Seized, captured.

n: Ezekiel addresses Zedekiah directly: “You profane, wicked prince of Israel, your day has come.”

f.g: King Zedekiah.

n: Remove the turban and take off the crown. Everything will be turned upside down: the lowly raised, the proud brought low.

f.g: A turban—possibly the high priest’s turban, suggesting both kingship and priesthood fail.

f.w: exalt him that is low, and abase him that is high

n: “A ruin, a ruin, a ruin!” Judah’s kingship will cease until the one comes to whom it rightfully belongs. Christians understand this as pointing to Jesus Christ, the rightful heir of David’s throne.

f.w: I will overturn, overturn, overturn, it
f.g: The threefold repeat expresses total ruin.

f.w: until he come whose right it is

n: Ammon, which escaped this time, should not gloat. The sword is drawn for it too.

f.g: Their taunting of Israel.

n: Ammon’s own false visions and lies promised safety, but they too will fall with the slain.

f.w: Whiles they see vanity unto thee
f.g: While false seers give you empty hopes.

n: Put the sword back—Ammon will be judged in its own homeland.

f.w: in the land of thy nativity
f.g: In its own country.

n: God will pour out his anger on Ammon and hand it over to brutal men skilled at destruction.

f.g: Savage, cruel men.

n: Ammon will be fuel for the fire and be forgotten. Unlike Israel, it receives no promise of restoration here; Ammon as a nation later vanished from history.

f.w: thou shalt be no more remembered
